title: Atoms Move, and No Cycle Runs Alone

scenes.tts: A blue crab in the Chesapeake Bay is built from atoms that were somewhere else before. No one has traced the atoms in one particular crab. But we can trace the routes those atoms could take. How does matter keep moving through ecosystems? And what happens when people change a cycle?
scenes.visual: A crab block with arrows coming in from question-mark boxes; carbon and nitrogen tokens ride the arrows; then the two questions appear.

scenes.tts: Carbon is in every sugar, fat and protein in your body. Photosynthesis is how plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Respiration is how cells break down sugar with oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Plants, animals and microbes all do it.
scenes.visual: Air box holds a carbon token; photosynthesis arrow carries it into a plant; respiration arrows carry carbon dioxide back to air from plant, animal and microbes.
scenes.narration: Carbon is in every sugar, fat and protein in your body. Photosynthesis is how plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Respiration is how cells break down sugar with oxygen and release carbon dioxide. Plants, animals and microbes all do it.

scenes.tts: Combustion is burning. It joins carbon with oxygen and releases carbon dioxide quickly. Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organisms by fungi and bacteria. Their respiration returns much of the carbon to the air. Ocean absorption is carbon dioxide dissolving into seawater at the surface. Carbon dioxide also comes back out.
scenes.visual: Air box stays; burning, dead organisms and ocean each get an arrow to or from the air.

scenes.tts: Water cycles too. Evaporation turns liquid water into vapor. Condensation turns vapor into cloud droplets. Precipitation returns water to the ground as rain or snow. Moving water carries nutrients such as nitrogen, along with sediment and germs. So a rainstorm in Pennsylvania can move nitrogen into the Susquehanna River, which flows into the Bay.
scenes.visual: Bay, cloud, farm and river blocks; arrows for evaporation, condensation, precipitation; runoff carries nitrogen, sediment and germ tokens down the river to the Bay.

scenes.tts: Your body uses nitrogen to build proteins and D N A. Air is about 78 percent nitrogen gas. But the two atoms in each molecule are held by a very strong bond. Most organisms cannot break it. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia. In nature, certain microbes, mostly bacteria, do most of it. Nitrification changes ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate. Assimilation is a plant taking up nitrate or ammonium. Ammonification is decomposers turning wastes and dead bodies back into ammonium. Denitrification is bacteria turning nitrate back into nitrogen gas.

scenes.tts: So how does matter keep moving? Atoms are not used up. They move between air, water, soil and living things, and they change form. People can change a cycle. Burning coal, oil and natural gas adds carbon to the air. That carbon was locked underground for millions of years. Water carries nitrogen from fields toward the Bay. No cycle runs alone.
